newsitem.title: ZAIRE: U.N. spotlights plight of Zaire refugees.
newsitem.headline: U.N. spotlights plight of Zaire refugees.

text.p: World attention focused on the plight of Rwandan Hutu civilians trapped in Zaire's war zone on Saturday after U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan expressed concern about the arming of Hutu hardliners in the main refugee encampment.
U.N. officials in New York said that Mohammed Sahnoun, the new special envoy for Central Africa, would convey Annan's concerns to the government when he arrived in Zaire on Saturday.
But a senior Kinshasa defence ministry official told Reuters that Zaire was not arming the Hutus, who have been blamed for the 1994 genocide in Rwanda of minority Tutsis.

"They say we have given weapons to the Hutu hardliners there but how can we do this when we have weaponry problems with our own troops," he said, adding that there was no fighting reported from the refugee area.

Up to 150,000 refugees occupy makeshift camps around the village of Tingi Tingi, about 200 km (125 miles) southeast of Zaire's third city of Kisangani, headquarters for army operations against Tutsi-led rebels advancing from the east.
Medical workers say up to 30 people a day are dying there from hunger or disease.
Annan has appealed to all parties "to stop turning the Tingi Tingi refugee camp into an armed base and to ensure the safety and security of all refugees and humanitarian personnel".
He said in a statement that former Hutu Rwandan soldiers and militias there were receiving arms and ammunition by air and were being sent to frontlines or deploying near the camps.
"This situation puts at risk the lives of innocent refugees and humanitarian workers in the area," he said, adding that young male refugees were being actively recruited.
Ethnic Tutsis launched the war in October, accusing the Zairean authorities of denying them citizenship and of plans to expel them to neighbouring Rwanda, their ancestral home.
They now hold towns and territory along the border with Rwanda, Burundi and Uganda.

Rebel thrusts on several fronts have blunted a much-touted counter-offensive the army launched on January 20 but the army says no major towns have fallen and it is reinforcing Kisangani and Buta to the north and Kindu to the south.
Rebel leader Laurent Kabila said he had ordered his forces to avoid the Tingi Tingi camp but diplomats in New York said the military build-up there could alter that plan.
Kabila has given President Mobutu Sese Seko, who has spent half of the last year in France recovering from prostate surgery, until February 21 to begin talks on stepping down.
The government on Friday banned public demonstrations until the end of the war and warned that anyone breaching the ban would deemed to be colluding with the enemy.
A strike call by the main opposition on Monday virtually shut down the usually teeming capital of five million people.
The main opposition Sacred Union of the Radical Opposition (USOR) of Etienne Tshisekedi called the strike to demand the removal of Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo.
USOR, which has called for negotiations with the rebels, denounced Kengo's conduct of the war and accused him of stalling on promised elections.
